claims.label: ABOUT 1 IN 4
claims.text: Bright light such as sunlight makes about one in four people sneeze (estimates vary).
claims.quote: Exposure to bright light such as sunlight elicits a sneeze or prickling sensation in about one of every four individuals; affecting approximately 25% of the population

claims.text: Aristotle asked why people sneeze after looking at the sun, and suggested the sun's heat sets up movement in the nose.
claims.quote: Why is it that one sneezes more after one has looked at the sun? Is it because the sun engenders heat and so causes movement; He hypothesized that the sun's heat caused sweating inside the nose

claims.text: In the 17th century Francis Bacon faced the sun with his eyes closed and did not sneeze, and concluded the cause was not the heating of the nostrils.
claims.quote: In the 17th century, English philosopher Francis Bacon disproved Aristotle's hypothesis by facing the sun with his eyes closed, which did not elicit the ordinary sneeze response; The cause is not the heating of the nostrils

claims.text: Bacon wrote in 1635 that the cause was 'the drawing down of the moisture of the brain'.
claims.quote: Francis Bacon thought he had the condition figured out in 1635; but the drawing down of the moisture of the brain

claims.text: Bacon's idea that watering eyes drained into the nose was later judged wrong too, because the sneeze comes too quickly.
claims.quote: scientists later determined this hypothesis to also be incorrect because sun-induced sneezing occurs too quickly after sunlight exposure

claims.text: A 2010 EEG study found that photic sneezers' visual cortex is generally more excitable to visual stimuli than other people's.
claims.quote: we found a generally enhanced excitability of the visual cortex (mainly in the cuneus) to visual stimuli in 'photic sneezers' compared with control subjects; Published: February 15, 2010

claims.text: A 2025 review says the underlying mechanisms are still unclear.
claims.quote: Despite its long history in scientific literature, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear

myths.myth: The sun's heat on your nose makes you sneeze (Aristotle).
myths.truth: Bacon faced the sun with his eyes closed and didn't sneeze: it's the light reaching the eyes.

open_questions: Exact mechanism unknown; script says so.
Prevalence varies by study (18-35%); labelled 'about 1 in 4'.
